---
title: "Road map"
---

How much do house prices rise when incomes rise? Take the 48 contiguous US
states and the District of Columbia, 1975 to 2003, and regress log house prices
on log income in each state. The average of the 49 slopes is 0.30: a 10% rise
in income goes with a 3% rise in prices. Now allow for one more thing. Every
state feels the same national forces, interest rates and credit conditions,
each to its own degree. With that allowed for, the elasticity is 1.14. Same
data, almost four times the answer [@holly2010; @croissant2019, pp. 197–199].
This book is about why.

A **panel** follows the same units, here states, over several periods. Its
promise is that each state is compared with itself over time, so everything
fixed about a state drops out. Its catch is that the states are not
independent of each other. A national shock moves them all at once, and in
the picture below it is hard to see 49 separate stories:

```{r}
#| label: c00-0-together
#| fig-cap: "Log house prices (left) and their annual growth (right) in 49
#|   US states, 1975–2003. Grey: one line per state. Black: the cross-state
#|   average. Prices are an index with 1980 = 100 in every state, which is
#|   why the lines pinch together in 1980."
#| fig-alt: "Two line charts with 49 thin grey lines and one thick black
#|   line each. On the left, log price indices rise and fall in waves that
#|   most states share, around the average. On the right, annual growth
#|   rates swing together: booms and busts hit most states in the same
#|   years, by different amounts."
data("HousePricesUS", package = "pder")
lp <- with(HousePricesUS, tapply(log(price), list(year, names), identity))
growth <- diff(lp)
op <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
graphics::matplot(as.numeric(rownames(lp)), lp, type = "l", lty = 1,
                  col = "grey75", xlab = "year", ylab = "log price index",
                  main = "Levels")
graphics::lines(as.numeric(rownames(lp)), rowMeans(lp), lwd = 3)
graphics::matplot(as.numeric(rownames(growth)), growth, type = "l", lty = 1,
                  col = "grey75", xlab = "year", ylab = "annual growth",
                  main = "Growth rates")
graphics::lines(as.numeric(rownames(growth)), rowMeans(growth), lwd = 3)
graphics::par(op)
```

In equations, state *i* in year *t* follows

$$
y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta x_{it} + u_{it}, \qquad
u_{it} = \lambda_i f_t + \varepsilon_{it}.
$$

Here $\alpha_i$ is everything fixed about the state, $f_t$ is the national
shock in year *t*, and $\lambda_i$ is how strongly state *i* feels it. Fixed
effects remove $\alpha_i$. Year effects remove $f_t$, but only if every state
feels it equally, $\lambda_i = 1$. When the loadings differ and the shock also
moves income, the shock leaks into $\hat\beta$. That leak is the gap between
0.30 and 1.14.

A panel analysis follows one workflow, not a fixed menu of tests. Build the
panel first, since its shape and balance limit every tool that comes after.
Then test whether units move together: dependence that is strong and global
calls for common factors, dependence that is weak and local calls for a
spatial model. Time dependence is a separate layer, asked once the
cross-sectional question is settled. Core panel models, fixed and random
effects among them, come last, once the error structure is known. The diagram
below maps the whole process; each box is a chapter.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  P["Build the panel<br/>shape, balance"] --> CD{"Do units move together?<br/>CD test"}
  CD -->|"no"| UR{"Do series wander?<br/>unit roots"}
  CD -->|"yes"| A{"How strong?<br/>exponent α"}
  A -->|"strong, global"| CF["Common factors:<br/>CCE"]
  A -->|"weak, local"| W["Spatial weights"]
  W --> SM["Spatial model:<br/>SAR / SEM, FE or RE"]
  CF --> UR
  SM --> UR
  UR -->|"yes, I(1)"| CO["Cointegration,<br/>or difference"]
  UR -->|"no, I(0)"| SC["Serial correlation,<br/>dynamic panels"]
  CO --> CORE["Core panel models:<br/>FE, RE, pooling"]
  SC --> CORE
```


**The chapters.**

1. **Explore the panel.** How many units, how many periods, and whether every
   unit is observed every period decide which tools apply
   ([panel shape](../01-explore/index.qmd#sec-panel-shape)).
2. **Cross-sectional dependence.** Do units move together more than chance
   allows? The CD test answers that
   ([CD tests](../02-cross-dependence/index.qmd#sec-csd-tests)), the
   exponent α says how strong
   ([α](../02-cross-dependence/index.qmd#sec-csd-exponent)), and when
   dependence is strong and global, common correlated effects removes it
   ([CCE](../02-cross-dependence/index.qmd#sec-cce)). This chapter gives the
   1.14 above.
3. **Spatial dependence.** When dependence is weak and local, neighbours
   matter more than the whole panel; still to come
   ([spatial dependence](../03-spatial/index.qmd)).
4. **Time dependence.** Do series wander with no level to return to
   ([why it matters](../04-time/index.qmd#sec-ur-why))? First-generation
   tests assume independent units
   ([first generation](../04-time/index.qmd#sec-ur-first-gen)),
   second-generation tests allow a common factor
   ([second generation](../04-time/index.qmd#sec-ur-second-gen)), and the
   fraction of series that reject the null needs its own test
   ([fraction](../04-time/index.qmd#sec-ur-fraction)), past a set of traps
   ([traps](../04-time/index.qmd#sec-ur-traps),
   [summary](../04-time/index.qmd#sec-ur-summary)). Cointegration, serial
   correlation and dynamic panels are still to come.
5. **Core panel models.** Fixed and random effects, pooling, and the tests
   between them close the process; still to come
   ([core panel models](../05-core/index.qmd)).
